sections.heading: Glass Is Cut for One Opening
body: A sheet of glass can't be trimmed to fit once it's made. Shower glass and most door glass is tempered, and tempered glass can't be cut at all after it's tempered.
So the measurement is the job. A bathroom wall that leans a quarter inch or a window frame that has shifted over the years is the difference between glass that drops in and glass that goes back.
That's why we come out and measure the opening ourselves instead of quoting from a guess. Then we cut the glass to that measurement and install it.

sections.heading: Frameless Shower Doors
body: If your shower has a curtain, or a framed door with a track that sticks and collects scum, a frameless door is the change you notice every morning.
There's no metal frame around the glass. The weight is carried by the hinges and the glass itself, so the fit has to be exact.
We measure in your bathroom, fit the door to the shower you have and install it. Frameless shower doors are the work we do most.

sections.heading: Walk-In Shower Glass
body: A walk-in shower trades the door for a fixed panel of glass and an open entry. It suits a bathroom where you want the tile to show and nothing to step around.
The panel has to sit where it will stop the spray from the shower head, so we measure with the head in mind, not just the width of the opening.
We install the glass and leave the bathroom clean.

sections.heading: Window Glass Replacement
body: A cracked pane, a window that fogged between the panes or a sash that's lost its glass doesn't always mean a new window. Often the frame is fine and the glass is the part that failed.
We replace the glass in the windows you have, one pane or a whole house worth. When a project calls for new windows or aluminum glass doors, we supply those too, from one opening to a long order.

sections.heading: Storefront and Commercial Glass
body: When a storefront pane breaks, the shop can't lock up and customers can't come in. That's a problem to fix this week, not next month.
We do commercial glass the way we do homes. We come out, measure the opening and install, so a business gets the same quick visit a homeowner does.

sections.heading: What Moves the Price of Glass
body: We don't put prices on a page, because glass isn't priced off a list. It's priced off your opening.

Size is the biggest factor, since more glass costs more. After that come the thickness of the glass, the hardware on a shower door, whether the edges are polished and whether the glass has to be tempered.
That's another reason we measure first. Once we've seen the opening and talked through what you want, the quote is for your job and not a range.

sections.heading: Why a Frameless Door Beats a Curtain or a Framed Slider
body: A shower curtain clings, grows mildew along the hem and lets water out when the fan pulls on it. A framed door has a bottom track that fills with soap scum and a roller that wears until the door scrapes.
A frameless door has no track and no metal frame around the glass. Thick tempered glass hangs from a few hinges, so there's less to clean and nothing for scum to hide in.
It also lets you see the tile. A small bathroom looks bigger when the shower isn't boxed in by a frame.

sections.heading: It Has to Be Measured in Your Bathroom
body: Frameless glass carries its own weight, so a quarter inch matters. Bathroom walls lean, tubs sit a little off level and tile adds thickness no drawing shows.
Glass can't be trimmed once it's made, and tempered glass can't be cut at all. If the door is made to a wrong number, it doesn't get fixed with a shim. It gets remade.
So we come to your bathroom and measure the real shower, not the one on the plans. Then we cut the glass to those numbers.

sections.heading: A Door or a Walk-In Panel
body: There are two ways to go, and the bathroom usually points to one.
**A hinged door** closes the shower in. It holds the heat and keeps the spray in a tub-shower combination or a small stall.
**Walk-in shower glass** is a fixed panel with an open entry and no door to swing. It suits a larger shower with room to step in, and it leaves the tile in view.
With a walk-in, the panel has to stand where the spray from the shower head would otherwise hit the floor. That's why we look at where the head points before we decide how wide the glass should be.
Not sure which way to go? Call the office and talk it through before the visit.

sections.quote: Excellent craftsmanship, and quick work. I really appreciate the great service while installing the walk-in shower, I would definitely work with them again, highly recommend them.

sections.heading: What Decides the Look and the Price
body: A shower door is mostly glass, so size drives the price first. After that come the thickness of the glass, the hinges and handle you pick and the finish on them.
Clear glass is the usual choice, and it's what lets the bathroom keep its light.
Hardware is also what wears. Hinges carry the full weight of the door, so they're worth choosing on purpose and not by the cheapest option.
Once we've measured and talked through the choices, you get a quote for your shower.

sections.heading: When It's the Glass That Failed
body: A cracked pane is obvious. Others are quieter: a haze between the two panes of a double-pane window that won't wipe off, or a window that has always felt cold to stand next to.
Fog between the panes means the seal around the sealed glass unit has failed and moisture got in. Cleaning won't reach it, because it's inside. The glass unit is what gets replaced.
Cracks come from a hit, from the house settling or from heat building up unevenly across the pane. Either way, the frame is often fine and the glass is the part that needs to go.

sections.heading: Glass or the Whole Window
body: Older single-pane windows fail by breaking. Newer double-pane windows fail by fogging, and nothing is cracked.
Either way, the question is the same: what's wrong with it, the glass or the frame?
Replacing only the glass is usually the faster, smaller job when the frame is straight, solid and still opens and closes well.
A whole window is the better call when the frame itself is the problem: rot, warping, a sash that doesn't close or a frame that has pulled out of square.
We look at the frame when we come out to measure, so you hear which one makes sense before you spend anything. And if the answer is new windows, we supply those too.

sections.heading: One Pane or Thirty
body: Some jobs are one cracked pane in the back bedroom. Some are every window in a building.
We handle both the same way. We come out, measure each opening and cut the glass to fit.
For larger projects we also supply windows and aluminum glass doors, so a single order can cover the glass, the windows and the doors.

sections.heading: Why Every Opening Gets Measured
body: Windows that look identical rarely are. Houses settle, frames get replaced one at a time and old openings drift out of square.
Glass can't be trimmed once it's made, so the number has to be right before the glass is cut. We measure the opening itself instead of assuming the neighbor window is the same.

Safety matters on some windows, too. Glass in a door, beside a door or low to the floor is usually required to be tempered safety glass, and tempered glass can't be cut after it's made. That's one more reason to measure first.
